Variance Bounds: Some Old and Some New

**Abstract**

For functions of independent random variables, various upper and lower variance bounds are revisited in diverse settings. These are then specialized to the Bernoulli, Gaussian, infinitely divisible cases and to Banach space valued random variables. Frameworks and techniques vary from jackknives through semigroups and beyond. Some new applications are presented, in particular, recovering and improving upon all the known estimates on the variance of the length of the longest common subsequences of two random words.

## 1 Introduction and preliminary results

We revisit below various lower and upper bounds on the variance of functions of independent random variables. Throughout and unless otherwise noted, \(X_1,\dots,X_n,X'_1,\dots,X'_n\) are independent random variables such that for all \(k\in\{1,\dots,n\}\), _X<sub>k</sub>_ and \(X'_k\) are identically distributed, while \(S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) is a Borel function such that \(\mathbb{E}S(X_1,\dots,X_n)^2<+\infty\). Next, and if _S_ is short for _S(X_<sub>1</sub>_,...,X<sub>n</sub>_), for any \(k\in\{1,\dots,n\}\), let \(S^k:=S(X_1,\dots,X_{k-1},X'_k,X_{k+1},\dots,X_n)\) and more generally if \(\alpha\subset\{1,\dots,n\}\), let \(S^\alpha\) be defined as _S(X_<sub>1</sub>_,...,X<sub>n</sub>_) but with _X<sub>k</sub>_ replaced by \(X'_k\) for all \(k\in\alpha\), and so \(S^\emptyset=S\), while \(S^{\{1,\dots,n\}}\) is an independent copy of _S_. With the help of these preliminary notations, we next recall the definitions of various quantities which will play an important role in the sequel.

Following [2], for \(k\in\{1,\dots,n\}\), let

\(B_k:=\mathbb{E}\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{i\in\mathfrak{S}_n}S(S^{i_1,\dots,i_{k-1}}-S^{i_1,\dots,i_k}),\) (1.1)

where S_<sub>n</sub>_ is the symmetric group of degree _n_ and where for _k_=1,\(S^{i_1,\dots,i_{k-1}}=S\). As the following sum is telescopic:

\(\sum_{k=1}^nB_k=\mathbb{E}\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{i\in\mathfrak{S}_n}S(S-S^{i_1,\dots,i_n})=\mathrm{Var}S.\)

One key fact motivating the definition of the _B<sub>k</sub>_’s is that they can be rewritten as:

\(B_k=\mathbb{E}\frac{1}{2n!}\sum_{i\in\mathfrak{S}_n}(S-S^{i_k})(S^{i_1,\dots,i_{k-1}}-S^{i_1,\dots,i_k}).\)

Indeed, if \(\alpha,\beta\subset\{1,\dots,n\}\),

\(\mathbb{E}\left(S^\alpha S^\beta\right)=\mathbb{E}\left(SS^{\alpha\Delta\beta}\right),\) (1.2)

where as usual \(\Delta\) denotes the symmetric difference operator, so

Next, for all \(k\in\{1,\dots,n\}\), let \(\Delta_kS:=S-S^k\), and for \(k\neq\ell\), let \(\Delta_{k,\ell} S:=\Delta_k(\Delta_\ell S)=S-S^k-S^\ell+S^{k,\ell}\) (note the commutativity property: \(\Delta_k(\Delta_\ell S)=\Delta_\ell(\Delta_kS)\)). Iterating this process, let \(\Delta_{i_1,\dots,i_k}S:=\Delta_k(\Delta_{i_1,\dots,i_{k-1}}S)\). Using this notation, we have

\(B_k=\mathbb{E}\frac{1}{2n!}\sum_{i\in\mathfrak{S}_n}(\Delta_{i_k}S)(\Delta_{i_k}S)^{i_1,\dots,i_{k-1}},\) (1.4)

and so \(B_k\ge 0\) since if \(U,U'\) and _V_ are independent with _U_ and \(U'\) identically distributed, then for any function _F_ such that _F(U,V_) is integrable, \(\mathbb{E}\left(F(U,V)F(U',V)\right)=\mathbb{E}\left(\mathbb{E}\left(F(U,V)|V\right)^2\right)\ge 0\). We are now ready to generalize the approach used to go from (1.1) to (1.4), leading to novel properties of the \(B'_ks\).

**Lemma 1.1.** _Let_ \(\alpha\neq\emptyset\) _and_ \(\beta\) _be two disjoint subsets of_ {1_,...,n}. Then,_

\(\mathbb{E}\left(S(\Delta_\alpha S)^\beta\right)=\frac{1}{2^{|\alpha|}}\mathbb{E}\left(\Delta_\alpha S(\Delta_\alpha S)^\beta\right).\) (1.5)

_Proof._ First, if \(\beta=\emptyset\), then the above identity reduces to (1.3). Next, by a straightforward induction on the cardinality \(k:=|\alpha|\), note that \(\Delta_\alpha S=\sum_{\alpha^\prime\subset\alpha}(-1)^{|\alpha^\prime|}S^{\alpha^\prime}\). Then, for any \(\alpha'\subset\alpha\),<tbc>

\((-1)^{|\alpha^\prime|}S^{\alpha^\prime}(\Delta_\alpha S)^\beta=\sum_{\alpha^{\prime\prime}\subset\alpha}(-1)^{|\alpha^\prime|+|\alpha^{\prime\prime}|}S^{\alpha^\prime} S^{\alpha^{\prime\prime}\cup\beta},\)

<tbc>and so using (1.2) (\(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are disjoint and \(\alpha'\subset\alpha\) so \(\alpha'\Delta(\alpha\cup\beta)=(\alpha'\Delta\alpha)\cup\beta\)),<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}\left((-1)^{|\alpha^\prime|}S^{\alpha^\prime}(\Delta_\alpha S)^\beta\right)=\mathbb{E}\left(\sum_{\alpha^{\prime\prime}\subset\alpha}(-1)^{|\alpha^\prime|+|\alpha^{\prime\prime}|}SS^{(\alpha^\prime\Delta_\alpha^{\prime\prime})\cup\beta}\right).\)

<tbc>Since \(\alpha''\mapsto\alpha'\Delta\alpha''\) is just a permutation of the subsets of \(\alpha\) and \((-1)^{\alpha^\prime\Delta_\alpha^{\prime\prime}}=(-1)^{|\alpha^\prime|+|\alpha^{\prime\prime}|}\),<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}\left((-1)^{|\alpha^\prime|}S^{\alpha^\prime}(\Delta_\alpha S)^\beta\right)=\mathbb{E}\left(\sum_{\alpha^{\prime\prime}\subset\alpha}(-1)^{|\alpha^{\prime\prime}|}SS^{\alpha^{\prime\prime}\cup\beta}\right)=\mathbb{E}\left(S(\Delta_\alpha S)^\beta\right),\)

<tbc>and so

\(\frac{1}{2^{|\alpha|}}\mathbb{E}\left(\Delta_\alpha S(\Delta_\alpha S)^\beta\right)=\frac{1}{2^{|\alpha|}}\sum_{\alpha^\prime\subset\alpha}\mathbb{E}\left((-1)^{|\alpha^\prime|}S^{\alpha^\prime}(\Delta_\alpha S)^\beta\right)=\mathbb{E}\left(S(\Delta_\alpha S)^\beta\right).\)

Let _T_ be the forward shift operator, i.e., for \(k\in\{1,\dots,n-1\}\), let _TB<sub>k</sub>_:=_B_<sub>_k_+1</sub> and let _D_ be the backward discrete derivative: _D_:=_Id-T_ (so for \(k\in\{1,\dots,n-1\}\), _DB<sub>k</sub>=B<sub>k</sub>-B_<sub>_k_+1</sub>), and denote by \(D^\ell\) (\(\ell\ge 1\)) its \(\ell\)-th iteration, with _D_<sup>0</sup>=_Id_. It is known (see \[2\]) that the finite sequence \((B_k)_{1\le k\le n}\) is non-increasing. More can be said.

**Theorem 1.2.** _For all_ \(\ell\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}\) _and_ \(k\in\{1,\dots,n-\ell\}\),

\(D^\ell B_k=\mathbb{E}\frac{1}{2^{\ell+1}n!}\sum_{i\in\mathfrak{S}_n}(\Delta_{i_1,\dots,i_{\ell+1}}S)(\Delta_{i_1,\dots,i_{\ell+1}}S)^{i_{\ell+2},\dots,i_{k+\ell}}.\) (1.6)

_In particular,_ \(D^\ell B_k\ge 0\)_, i.e.,_ \((B_k)_{1\le k\le n}\) _is completely monotone (recall that D=Id-T)._

_Proof._ With the previous lemma, it is enough to prove that for all \(\ell\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}\) and \(k\in\{1,\dots,n-\ell\}\),<tbc>

\(D^\ell B_k=\mathbb{E}\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{i\in\mathfrak{S}_n}S(\Delta_{i_1,\dots,i_{\ell+1}}S)^{i_{\ell+2},\dots,i_{k+\ell}}.\) (1.7)

This is done by induction on \(\ell\). When \(\ell=0\), (1.7) is just the very definition of _Bk_. Assume next that (1.7) holds for \(\ell\in\{0,\dots,n-2\}\). Let \(k\in\{1,\dots,n-(\ell+1)\}\). Then, \(D^{\ell+1}B_k=\mathbb{E}\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{i\in\mathfrak{S}_n}S(\Delta_{i_1,\dots,i_{\ell+1}}S)^{i_{\ell+2},\dots,i_{k+\ell}}-\mathbb{E}\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{i\in\mathfrak{S}_n}S(\Delta_{i_1,\dots,i_{\ell+1}}S)^{i_{\ell+2},\dots,i_{k+1+\ell}}\)
\(=\mathbb{E}\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{i\in\mathfrak{S}_n}S(\Delta_{i_1,\dots,i_{\ell+1}}S)^{i_{\ell+3},\dots,i_{k+1+\ell}}-\mathbb{E}\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{i\in\mathfrak{S}_n}S(\Delta_{i_1,\dots,i_{\ell+1}}S)^{i_{\ell+2},\dots,i_{k+1+\ell}}\)
\(=\mathbb{E}\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{i\in\mathfrak{S}_n}S(\Delta_{i_1,\dots,i_{\ell+2}}S)^{i_{\ell+3},\dots,i_{k+1+\ell}},\) where in getting the second equality, the terms are reindexed. We wish now to study potential connections between the _Bk_’s and jackknives operators _Jk_ and _Kk_ previously studied in \[4\]. For \(Y\in\sigma(X_1,\dots,X_n)\), i.e., Y measurable with respect to the \(\sigma\)-field generated by _X_1_,...,Xn_ and \(i\in\{1,\dots,n\}\), let E(_i_)_Y_:=E(_Y|X_1_,...,X__i_-1_,X__i_+1_,...,Xn_) (with the convention E(0)_Y_:=_Y_) and more generally for any subset \(\alpha\) of {1_,...,n_}, let \(\mathbb{E}^\alpha Y:=\mathbb{E}(Y|(X_j)_{j\notin\alpha}),\) with \(\mathbb{E}^\emptyset Y=Y\) , and E{1_,...,n_}_Y_=E_Y_ . Next, for \(i\in\{1,\dots,n\}\), let \(\mathrm{Var}^{(i)}Y:=\mathbb{E}^{(i)}Y^2-(\mathbb{E}^{(i)}Y)^2\) while iterating, for \(i\in\mathfrak{S}_n\), and \(k\ge 1\), let \(\mathrm{Var}^{(i_1,\dots,i_k)}Y:=\mathbb{E}^{(i_1)}(\mathrm{Var}^{(i_2,\dots,i_k)}Y)-\mathrm{Var}^{(i_2,\dots,i_k)}(\mathbb{E}^{(i_1)}Y),\) and so (using the commutation property of conditional expectations) for any \(\alpha=\{i_1,\dots,i_k\}\), \(\mathrm{Var}^\alpha Y\) is well defined. For \(k\in\{1,\dots,n\}\), let \(J_k:=\mathbb{E}\sum_{i_1\neq i_2\dots\neq i_k}\mathrm{Var}^{(i_1,\dots,i_k)}S,\) and \(K_k:=\mathbb{E}\sum_{i_1\neq i_2\dots\neq i_k}\mathrm{Var}^{(i_1,\dots,i_k)}\mathbb{E}^\overline{(i_1,\dots,i_k)}S,\) where (_i_1_,...,ik_)=(_i__k_+1_,...,in_). For ease of notation, set also \(J'_k:=J_k/k!\) and \(K'_k:=K_k/k!\). The next lemma provides relationships between these quantities and the _Bk_’s, it allows to easily get, and in a unified fashion, many of the known expressions involving the variance, along with some new ones. **Lemma 1.3.** _Let_ \(\alpha\neq\emptyset\) _and_ \(\beta\) _be two disjoint subsets of_ {1_,...,n}. Then_ \(\mathbb{E}\left(\mathrm{\textit{Var}}^\alpha\mathbb{E}^\beta S\right)=\mathbb{E}\left(S(\Delta_\alpha S)^\beta\right).\) (1.8) _Proof._ If \(\beta=\emptyset\), then the result is clear. Next, the proof is done by induction on the cardinality of \(\alpha\). For the base case, let \(|\alpha|=1\), i.e., let \(\alpha=\{i\}\), for some \(i\in\{1,\dots,n\}\). Then, \(\mathbb{E}\left(\mathrm{Var}^{(i)}\mathbb{E}^\beta S\right)=\mathbb{E}\left(\mathbb{E}^{(i)}(\mathbb{E}^\beta S)^2-(\mathbb{E}^{(i)}\mathbb{E}^\beta S)^2\right)\)
\(=\mathbb{E}(\mathbb{E}^\beta S)^2-\mathbb{E}(\mathbb{E}^{\beta,i}S)^2\)
\(=\mathbb{E}(SS^\beta)-\mathbb{E}(SS^{\beta,i})\)
\(=\mathbb{E}(S(\Delta_iS)^\beta),\) where to get the next to last equality we use \(\mathbb{E}(SS^\beta)=\mathbb{E}(\mathbb{E}^\beta(SS^\beta))=\mathbb{E}(\mathbb{E}^\beta S)^2\), which follows from the independence assumption. Now, let us assume the validity of the lemma for any set of cardinality _k_ and let \(\alpha=\{i_1,\dots,i_{k+1}\}\).

Then, since \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are disjoint, and by independence, \(\mathbb{E}\left(\mathrm{Var}^\alpha\mathbb{E}^\beta S\right)=\mathbb{E}\left(\mathbb{E}^{(i_1)}(\mathrm{Var}^{(i_2,\dots,i_{k+1})}\mathbb{E}^\beta S)-\mathrm{Var}^{(i_2,\dots,i_{k+1})}(\mathbb{E}^{(i_1)}\mathbb{E}^\beta S)\right)\)
\(=\mathbb{E}\left(\mathrm{Var}^{(i_2,\dots,i_{k+1})}\mathbb{E}^\beta S\right)-\mathbb{E}\left(\mathrm{Var}^{(i_2,\dots,i_{k+1})}\mathbb{E}^{(i)}S\mathbb{E}^\beta S\right)\)
\(=\mathbb{E}\left(S(\Delta_{(i_2,\dots,i_{k+1})}S)^\beta\right)-\mathbb{E}\left(S(\Delta_{(i_2,\dots,i_{k+1})}S)^{\beta,i}\right)\)
\(=\mathbb{E}(S(\Delta_\alpha S)^\beta),\) where in the middle equality we have used the induction hypothesis. Recalling (1.7), we get from (1.8) that for all \(k\in\{1,\dots,n\}\), \(J'_k=\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{k}D^{k-1}B_1\text{and}K'_k=\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{k}D^{k-1}B_{n-k+1}.\) (1.9) It is easy to check that for any finite sequence \((a_k)_{1\le k\le n}\) and any positive integers \(k\in\{1,\dots,n\}\), \(a_k=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(-1)^j\genfrac(){pt}{2}{k-1}{j}D^ja_1=\sum_{j=0}^{n-k}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n-k}{j}D^ja_{n-j}.\) (1.10) In particular, for all \(k\in\{1,\dots,n\}\), \(B_k=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(-1)^j\frac{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{k-1}{j}}{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{j+1}}J'_{j+1},\) (1.11) \(B_k=\sum_{j=0}^{n-k}\frac{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n-k}{j}}{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{j+1}}K'_{j+1}.\) (1.12) We can now connect the \(J'_k\)’s and \(K'_k\)’s to the variance. **Lemma 1.4.** _For all_ \(k\in\{1,\dots,n\}\), \(\mathrm{\textit{Var}}S-J'_1+J'_2-\cdots+(-1)^kJ'_k=(-1)^k\sum_{1\le i_1<\cdots \(=(-1)^k\sum_{1\le i_1<\cdots \(=(-1)^k\sum_{1\le i_1<\cdots \(=(-1)^{k+1}\sum_{1\le i_0

The proof of (1.14) is very similar and so it is omitted. The following proposition recovers and extends some of the results obtained in \[4\]. **Proposition 1.5.** \(\text{\textit{Var}}S=J'_1-J'_2+\cdots+(-1)^{n-1}J'_n=K'_1+K'_2+\cdots+K'_n,\) (1.15) _and for all_ \(k\in\{1,\dots,n-1\}\), \(K'_{k+1}\le(-1)^k\left(\text{\textit{Var}}S-J'_1+J'_2-\cdots+(-1)^kJ'_k\right)\le J'_{k+1},\)
\(K'_{k+1}\le\text{\textit{Var}}S-K'_1-K'_2-\cdots-K'_k\le J'_{k+1}.\)
\(\text{\textit{Var}}S=J'_1-J'_2+\cdots+(-1)^{k-1}J'_k+(-1)^k\sum_{j=k+1}^n\genfrac(){pt}{2}{j-1}{k}K'_j.\) (1.16) \(\text{\textit{Var}}S=\frac{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{k}{1}}{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{1}}J'_1-\frac{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{k}{2}}{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{2}}J'_2+\cdots+(-1)^{k-1}\frac{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{k}{k}}{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{k}}J'_k+\frac{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n-k}{1}}{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{1}}K'_1+\frac{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n-k}{2}}{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{2}}K'_2+\cdots+\frac{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n-k}{n-k}}{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{n-k}}K'_{n-k}.\) (1.17) _Proof._ Above, the first two equalities simply follow from the fact that the right-hand terms in Lemma 1.4 are zero when _k=n_. Then, the first two inequalities follow from Lemma 1.4 and the complete monotonicity of the _Bk_’s: for \(1\le i_1\le n-k\), \(D^kB_{n-k}\le D^kB_{i_1}\le D^kB_1\). Let us turn to the identity (1.16). Applying the inversion formula (1.10) to \((D^kB_i)_{1\le i\le n-k}\), with \(i\le n-k\), we get \(\sum_{1\le i_1<\cdots \(=\sum_{i=1}^{n-k}\sum_{j=0}^{n-k-i}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n-i}{k}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n-k-i}{j}D^{k+j}B_{n-k-j}\)
\(=\sum_{i=1}^{n-k}\sum_{j=0}^{n-k-i}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n-i}{k}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n-k-i}{j}\frac{K'_{k+j+1}}{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{k+j+1}}\)
\(=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n-k-j}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n-i}{k+j}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{k+j}{k}\frac{K'_{k+j+1}}{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{k+j+1}}\)
\(=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{k+j}{k}K'_{k+j+1},\) where the last equality stems from the hockey-stick formula and reindexing. To finish, let us prove (1.17) which will follow from \(\text{Var}S=B_1+\cdots+B_k+B_{k+1}+\cdots+B_n\). Indeed, the equality (1.15) remains valid for any sequence \((a_n)_{n\ge 1}\), namely, the same proof shows that \(a_1+\cdots+a_n=\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{1}D^0a_1-\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{2}D^1a_1+\cdots+(-1)^{n-1}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{n}{n}D^{n-1}a_1.\) In particular, \(B_1+\cdots+B_k=\genfrac(){pt}{2}{k}{1}D^0B_1-\genfrac(){pt}{2}{k}{2}D^1B_1+\cdots+(-1)^{k-1}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{k}{k}D^{k-1}B_1\)
\(=\frac{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{k}{1}}{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{1}}J'_1-\frac{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{k}{2}}{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{2}}J'_2+\cdots+(-1)^{k-1}\frac{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{k}{k}}{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{k}}J'_k.\) The second part, \(B_{k+1}+\cdots+B_n\), is treated similarly.

The equality (1.17) could be of use to find the order of Var_S_ as _n_ tends to infinity. For example, if there is a constant _C\>_1 (independent of _n_) such that \(J'_2(n)\le CJ'_1(n)\), then, taking \(k=\lfloor\frac{n}{2C}\rfloor\) will lead to \(liminf_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\mathrm{Var}S(n)}{J'_1(n)}\ge\frac{1}{4C}.\) We have proved that the finite sequence \((B_k)_{1\le k\le n}\) is completely monotone and we already knew from \[2\] that it is non-increasing, so it is natural to wonder if one could find further properties of the _Bk_’s. On the other hand, one may also wonder whether or not \((K_k)_{1\le k\le n}\) does satisfy any further property except, of course, from being non-negative. Both answers appear to be negative: **Proposition 1.6.** _For any_ \(a_1,\dots,a_n\ge 0\)_, there exists_ \(S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) _a Borel function such that for all_ \(k\in\{1,\dots,n\}\)_, Kk=ak._ **Corollary 1.7.** _If_ \((b_k)_{1\le k\le n}\) _is completely monotone, then there exists_ \(S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) _a Borel function such that for all_ \(k\in\{1,\dots,n\}\)_, Bk=bk._ _Proof of the Corollary._ It is easy to see that \((b_k)_{1\le k\le n}\) is completely monotone if and only if for all \(k\in\{1,\dots,n\}\), \(D^{k-1}b_{n-k+1}\ge 0\). From the statement of the proposition, there exists \(S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) a Borel function such that for all \(k\in\{1,\dots,n\}\), \(K_k=\frac{n!}{(n-k)!}D^{k-1}b_{n-k+1}\), and, recalling (1.9), since there is no choice for the _Bk_’s knowing the _Kk_’s, _Bk=bk_. _Proof of the proposition._ This follows from using the link with the Hoeffding decomposition observed in \[4\]. Consider for example \(A_1,\dots,A_n\ge 0\) and \(S(X_1,\dots,X_n):=A_1\sum_{1\le i_1 \(=A_k^2k!\sum_{1\le i_1<\cdotsk_’s to have the _Kk_’s as wanted. One could expect the _Jk_’s to behave like the _Kk_’s and to also be able to take any values, but this is unfortunately not the case, for example \(2J_2/n=(n-1)(B_1-B_2)\le nB_1=J_1\). To conclude this section, we connect the _Bk_’s and the quantities _TA_ introduced in \[5\]. For any subset _A_ of {1_,...,n_}, including \(A=\emptyset\), _TA_ is defined as \(T_A=\sum_{j\notin A}\Delta_jS(\Delta_jS)^A,\) and then _T_ is defined as \(T=\sum_{A\unknown\{1,\dots,n\}}\frac{T_A}{2(n-|A|)\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{|A|}}.\) It is easy to check that for all \(k\in\{1,\dots,n\}\), \(B_k=\sum_{A:|A|=k-1}\frac{\mathbb{E}(T_A)}{2(n-|A|)\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{|A|}},\) hence \(\mathbb{E}T=\sum_{k=1}^nB_k=\mathrm{Var}S\) (as expected). **Remark 1.8.** (_i)_ _One might wonder if the above variance results can be transferred to the_ \(\Phi\)_-entropy. Let_ \(\Phi\) _be a convex function of the real variable such that_ \(\mathbb{E}|\Phi(S)|<+\infty\)_, and let the_ \(\Phi\)_-entropy_ \(H_\Phi\) _of S (e.g., see \[3\]) be defined as:_ \(H_\Phi(S)=\mathbb{E}\Phi(S)-\Phi(\mathbb{E}S).\)

_Following \[4\], for_ \(i\in\{1,\dots,n\}\)_, let_ \(H_\Phi^{(i)}(S)=\mathbb{E}^{(i)}\Phi(S)-\Phi(\mathbb{E}^{(i)}(S)),\) _while for_ \(i\neq j\in\{1,\dots,n\}\), \(H_\Phi^{(j,i)}(S):=\mathbb{E}^{(j)}H_\Phi^{(i)}(S)-H_\Phi^{(i)}(\mathbb{E}^{(j)}S)=H_\Phi^{(i,j)}(S).\) _Still iterating, for_ \(i_1\neq\dots\neq i_k\in\{1,\dots,n\}\), \(H_\Phi^{(i_1,\dots,i_k)}(S):=\mathbb{E}^{(i_1)}H_\Phi^{(i_2,\dots,i_k)}(S)-H_\Phi^{(i_2,\dots,i_k)}(\mathbb{E}^{(i_1)}S).\) _Define the corresponding Bk’s as,_ \(B_k:=\mathbb{E}\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{i\in\mathfrak{S}_n}H_\Phi^{(i_k)}(\mathbb{E}^{(i_1,\dots,i_{k-1})}S),\) _for all_ \(k\in\{1,\dots,n\}\)_. Once again the sum is telescopic:_ \(\sum_{k=1}^nB_k=\mathbb{E}\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{i\in\mathfrak{S}_n}\mathbb{E}^{(i_k)}\Phi(\mathbb{E}^{(i_1,\dots,i_{k-1})}S)-\Phi(\mathbb{E}^{(i_1,\dots,i_k)}S)=H_\Phi S.\) _By the conditional Jensen inequality, the Bk’s are non-negative. Just like in the variance case, it is clear by induction that for all_ \(\ell\in\{0,\dots,n-1\}\), \(D^\ell B_k=\mathbb{E}\frac{1}{n!}\sum_{i\in\mathfrak{S}_n}H_\Phi^{(i_1,\dots,i_{\ell+1})}(\mathbb{E}^{(i_{\ell+2},\dots,i_{k+\ell})}S).\) _Let us now look for the class of convex functions_ \(\Phi\) _such that for any S and X_1_,...,Xn satisfying the basic independence and integrability assumptions,_ \((B_k)_{1\le k\le n}\) _is non-increasing. In particular, for any random variable Z defined on a product space_ \(\Omega_1\times\Omega_2\) _satisfying the integrability conditions, choosing S and X_1_,...,Xn such that S=Z (S=f(X_1_,X_2) _for some function f), we have that_ \(D^1B_k=\frac{1}{n!}\mathbb{E}\sum_{i\in\mathfrak{S}_n}H_\Phi^{(i_1,i_2)}(\mathbb{E}^{(i_3,\dots,i_{k+1})}S)\)
\(=\frac{2}{n!}\mathbb{E}H_\Phi^{(1,2)}(S)\)

## 4 On the variance of the length of longest common subsequences

To finish these notes, we present some applications of the above inequalities to subsequences problems, in particular to lower-bounding the variance of the length of the longest common subsequences between two random words. For (_x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>s</sub>_), (_y_<sub>1</sub>_,...,y<sub>t</sub>_) two sequences taking values in a finite set A, we denote by \(LCS(x_1\cdots x_s;y_1\cdots y_t)\) the largest integer _k_ such that there exists \(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le s\), \(1\le j_1<\cdots<j_k\le t\) satisfying _a_<sub>_i_<sub>1</sub></sub>=_b_<sub>_j_<sub>1</sub></sub>_,...,a<sub>i<sub>k</sub></sub>=b<sub>j<sub>k</sub></sub>_, or 0 if there is no such integer. In the sequel, we take A={1_,...,m_} (for some _m_ we specify in each case), _X_<sub>1</sub>_,...,X<sub>n</sub>,...Y_<sub>1</sub>_,...,Y<sub>n</sub>,..._ i.i.d. random variables taking values in A (according to a distribution we specify), and consider the length of the longest common subsequences of these two random words, written \(LCS(X_1\cdots X_n;Y_1\cdots Y_n)\) or simply _LC<sub>n</sub>_.

### 4.1 A generic upper bound

Via the Efron-Stein inequality, the upper bound \(\mathrm{Var}S\le nB_1\) was already obtained \[21\]. Let us study the variance of _LC<sub>n</sub>_ with our approach.

Let now _Z_<sub>1</sub>_,...,Z_<sub>2_n_</sub> be _i.i.d._ Bernoulli random variables of parameter 1/2, and consider the _B<sub>k</sub>_’s of the function \(S(Z_1,\dots,Z_{2n}):=LCS(Z_1\cdots Z_{2n})=LC_n\). We know that \(\mathrm{Var}LC_n\le 2nB_1(2n)\). Using (3.6), \(B_1(2n)\le 1/4\) so \(\mathrm{Var}LC_n\le n/2\) (at result already known to \[21\]. But this last bound can be slightly improved: note that by symmetry of the zeros and ones in _LC<sub>n</sub>_ (that is, if \(\bar{Z}_i:=1-Z_i,i\in\{1,\dots,2n\}\), \(S(Z)=S(\bar{Z})\)), \(\mathbb{E}\tau_iS\)=0 so _B_<sub>2_n_</sub>(2_n_)=0. By convexity, \(B_1(2n)+\cdots+B_{2n}(2n)\le 2n(B_1(2n)+B_{2n}(2n))/2\), so \(\mathrm{Var}LC_n\le n/4\).

In case of an alphabet {1_,...,m_}, conditioning on \(X_i\neq X'_i\) we get \(B_1(2n)\le\left(1-\sum_{k=1}^mp_k^2\right)/2\), and when additionally _B_<sub>2_n_</sub>(2_n_)=0, then \(\mathrm{Var}LC_n\le\left(1-\sum_{k=1}^mp_k^2\right)n/2\), which improves, by a factor of two, on the upper bound obtained in \[21\] (see also \[13\]). The condition _B_<sub>2_n_</sub>(2_n_)=0 is realized, for instance, when \(p_1=\cdots=p_m=1/m\) (by symmetry).

In the remaining part of this manuscript, we focus on various lower bounds on the variance of _LC<sub>n</sub>_. Since by Theorem 1.2, \((B_k)_{1\le k\le 2n}\) is, in particular, non-decreasing,

\(\mathrm{Var}LC_n\ge 2nB_{2n},\) (4.1)

and this last inequality we will of use throughout this section. As a first instance, \[19, Theorem 2.1\] provides a lower bound on the variance of _LC<sub>n</sub>_, in the Bernoulli case, proving that when _p_ is smaller than some universal (but unspecified and extremely small) constant, the variance is of order _n_, see also \[13\] for more explicit bounds. To obtain this results, the authors of \[19\] first show Theorem 2.2 there, and then prove that it implies a variance lower bound of order _n_. The proof of this implication is long and we aim to show that the jackknives tools we developed greatly simplifies it. (This methodology also simplifies, in the quadratic case, the implication of \[13, Theorem 2.1\] towards the linear lower bound.) With our approach, we also generalize results for the case where one letter is omitted. We also proceed to prove, in the binary case, another slightly weaker bound: for some \(p_1\in(0.096,0.5)\) (so not as small as in \[19\] or \[13\]), or \(p_2\in(0.5,0.904)\), \(\mathrm{limsup}_{n\rightarrow+\infty}\mathrm{Var}LC_n/n>0\). Finally, we give further partial results on the order of the variance in the uniform case.
